In [[graph theory]], the '''Kneser graph''' {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} (alternatively {{math|''KG''<sub>''n'',''k''</sub>}}) is the [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] whose [[vertex (graph theory)|vertices]] correspond to the [[combination|{{mvar|k}}-element subsets of a set of {{mvar|n}} elements]], and where two vertices are adjacent [[if and only if]] the two corresponding sets are [[disjoint sets|disjoint]]. Kneser graphs are named after [[Martin Kneser]], who first investigated them in 1956.

== Examples ==
[[File:Kneser graph KG(7,3).jpg|thumb|Kneser graph {{math|1=''O''<sub>4</sub> = ''K''(7, 3)}}]]

The Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', 1)}} is the [[complete graph]] on {{mvar|n}} vertices.

The Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', 2)}} is the [[complement graph|complement]] of the [[line graph]] of the complete graph on {{mvar|n}} vertices.

The Kneser graph {{math|''K''(2''n'' − 1, ''n'' − 1)}} is the [[odd graph]] {{math|''O<sub>n</sub>''}}; in particular {{math|1=''O''<sub>3</sub> = ''K''(5, 2)}} is the [[Petersen graph]] (see top right figure).

The Kneser graph {{math|1=''O''<sub>4</sub> = ''K''(7, 3)}}, visualized on the right.

== Properties ==

=== Basic properties ===
The Kneser graph <math>K(n,k)</math> has <math>\tbinom{n}{k}</math> vertices. Each vertex has exactly <math>\tbinom{n-k}{k}</math> neighbors.

The Kneser graph is [[vertex-transitive graph|vertex transitive]] and [[Symmetric graph|arc transitive]]. When <math>k=2</math>, the Kneser graph is a [[strongly regular graph]], with parameters <math>( \tbinom{n}{2}, \tbinom{n-2}{2}, \tbinom{n-4}{2}, \tbinom{n-3}{2} )</math>. However, it is not strongly regular when <math>k>2</math>, as different pairs of nonadjacent vertices have different numbers of common neighbors depending on the size of the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the corresponding pairs of sets.

Because Kneser graphs are [[regular graph|regular]] and [[edge-transitive graph|edge-transitive]], their [[k-vertex-connected graph|vertex connectivity]] equals their [[degree (graph theory)|degree]], except for <math>K(2k,k)</math> which is [[connectivity (graph theory)|disconnected]]. More precisely, the connectivity of <math>K(n,k)</math> is <math>\tbinom{n-k}{k},</math> the same as the number of neighbors per vertex.{{sfnp|Watkins|1970}}

=== <span class="anchor" id="chromatic"></span>Chromatic number ===
As {{harvs|last=Kneser|year=1956|txt}} [[conjecture]]d, the [[chromatic number]] of the Kneser graph <math>K(n,k)</math> for <math>n\geq 2k</math> is exactly {{math|''n'' − 2''k'' + 2}}; for instance, the Petersen graph requires three colors in any [[proper coloring]]. This conjecture was [[mathematical proof|proved]] in several ways.

*[[László Lovász]] proved this in 1978 using [[topology|topological]] methods,{{sfnp|Lovász|1978}} giving rise to the field of [[topological combinatorics]].
*Soon thereafter [[Imre Bárány]] gave a simple proof, using the [[Borsuk–Ulam theorem]] and a lemma of [[David Gale]].{{sfnp|Bárány|1978}}
*Joshua E. Greene won the 2002 [[Morgan Prize]] for outstanding undergraduate research for his further-simplified but still topological proof.{{sfnp|Greene|2002}}
*In 2004, [[Jiří Matoušek (mathematician)|Jiří Matoušek]] found a purely [[combinatorial proof]].{{sfnp|Matoušek|2004}}
In contrast, the [[fractional chromatic number]] of these graphs is <math>n/k</math>.{{sfnp|Godsil|Meagher|2015}}
When <math>n< 2k</math>, <math>K(n,k)</math> has no edges and its chromatic number is 1. When <math>n=2k</math>, the graph is a perfect matching and its chromatic number is 2.

=== Hamiltonian cycles ===
It is well-known that the [[Petersen graph]] is not [[Hamiltonian graph|Hamiltonian]], but it was long conjectured that this was the sole exception and that every other connected Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} is Hamiltonian.

In 2003, Ya-Chen Chen showed that the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} contains a [[Hamiltonian cycle]] if{{sfnp|Chen|2003}}
:<math>n \geq \frac{1}{2} \left(3k+1+\sqrt{5k^2-2k+1} \right).</math>
Since
:<math>\frac{1}{2} \left (3k+1+\sqrt{5k^2-2k+1} \right )< \left (\frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \right) k+1</math>
holds for all <math>k</math>, this condition is satisfied if
:<math>n \geq  \left(\frac{3 + \sqrt{5}}{2} \right) k+1 \approx 2.62k+1.</math>
Around the same time, Shields showed (computationally) that, except the Petersen graph, all connected Kneser graphs {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} with {{math|''n'' ≤ 27}} are Hamiltonian.{{sfnp|Shields|2004}}

In 2021, Mütze, Nummenpalo, and Walczak proved that the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} contains a Hamiltonian cycle if there exists a non-negative [[integer]] <math>a</math> such that <math>n=2k+2^a</math>.{{sfnp|Mütze|Nummenpalo|Walczak|2021}} In particular, the [[odd graph]] {{mvar|O<sub>n</sub>}} has a Hamiltonian cycle if {{math|''n'' ≥ 4}}.  Finally, in 2023, Merino, Mütze and Namrata completed the proof of the conjecture.{{sfnp|Merino|Mütze|Namrata|2023}}

=== Cliques ===
When {{math|''n'' < 3''k''}}, the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} contains no triangles. More generally, when {{math|''n'' < ''ck''}} it does not contain [[clique (graph theory)|clique]]s of size {{math|''c''}}, whereas it does contain such cliques when {{math|''n'' ≥ ''ck''}}. Moreover, although the Kneser graph always contains [[cycle (graph theory)|cycle]]s of length four whenever {{math|''n'' ≥ 2''k'' + 2}}, for values of {{mvar|n}} close to {{math|2''k''}} the shortest [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] cycle may have variable length.{{sfnp|Denley|1997}}

=== Diameter ===
The [[Diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] of a connected Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} is{{sfnp|Valencia-Pabon|Vera|2005}}
<math display=block>\left\lceil \frac{k-1}{n-2k} \right\rceil + 1.</math>

===Spectrum===
The [[graph spectrum|spectrum]] of the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} consists of ''k'' + 1 distinct [[eigenvalue]]s: 
<math display=block>\lambda_j=(-1)^j\binom{n-k-j}{k-j}, \qquad j=0, \ldots,k.</math>
Moreover <math>\lambda_j</math> occurs with [[Multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicity]] <math>\tbinom{n}{j}-\tbinom{n}{j-1}</math> for <math>j >0</math> and <math>\lambda_0</math> has multiplicity 1.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.math.caltech.edu/~2011-12/2term/ma192b/kneser-evals.pdf |title=Archived copy |website=www.math.caltech.edu |access-date=9 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120323231232/http://www.math.caltech.edu/~2011-12/2term/ma192b/kneser-evals.pdf |archive-date=23 March 2012 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Chowdhury |first1=Ameerah Naz |title=Shadows and Intersections (PhD Thesis) |date=2012 |location=University of California, San Diego |page=47 |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/03k1h0m5 |access-date=21 May 2025}}</ref>

=== Independence number ===
The [[Erdős–Ko–Rado theorem]] states that the [[independence number]] of the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} for <math>n\geq 2k</math> is
<math display=block>\alpha(K(n,k))=\binom{n-1}{k-1},</math>
but if <math>n > 10000k</math>, then every vertex subset <math>S</math> of size beyond the independence number will contain a vertex adjacent to at least 
<math display=block>\left(\frac{1}{2}-O\left(\sqrt{\frac{k}{n}}\right)\right) \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}</math>
other vertices in <math>S</math>.{{sfnp|Chau|Ellis|Friedgut|Lifshitz|2025}}

== Related graphs ==
The '''[[Johnson graph]]''' {{math|''J''(''n'', ''k'')}} is the graph whose vertices are the {{mvar|k}}-element subsets of an {{mvar|n}}-element set, two vertices being adjacent when they meet in a {{math|(''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1)}}-element set. The Johnson graph {{math|''J''(''n'', 2)}} is the complement of the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', 2)}}. Johnson graphs are closely related to the [[Johnson scheme]], both of which are named after [[Selmer M. Johnson]].

The '''generalized Kneser graph''' {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'', ''s'')}} has the same vertex set as the Kneser graph {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}}, but connects two vertices whenever they correspond to sets that intersect in {{mvar|s}} or fewer items.{{sfnp|Denley|1997}} Thus {{math|1=''K''(''n'', ''k'', 0) = ''K''(''n'', ''k'')}}.

The '''bipartite Kneser graph''' {{math|''H''(''n'', ''k'')}} has as vertices the sets of {{mvar|k}} and {{math|''n'' − ''k''}} items drawn from a collection of {{mvar|n}} elements. Two vertices are connected by an edge whenever one set is a subset of the other.  Like the Kneser graph it is vertex transitive with degree <math>\tbinom{n-k}{k}.</math> The bipartite Kneser graph can be formed as a [[bipartite double cover]] of {{math|''K''(''n'', ''k'')}} in which one makes two copies of each vertex and replaces each edge by a pair of edges connecting corresponding pairs of vertices.{{sfnp|Simpson|1991}} The bipartite Kneser graph {{math|''H''(5, 2)}} is the [[Desargues graph]] and the bipartite Kneser graph {{math|''H''(''n'', 1)}} is a [[crown graph]].
